title: GitHub and RStudio Workflow Guide
text:
Copy the repository URL Navigate to the main project repository on GitHub. Click the green Code button and copy the repository URL (use HTTPS if you use a Personal Access Token, or SSH if you use SSH keys).
Start a Version Control project in RStudio Open RStudio on your laptop. Navigate to File > New Project… in the top menu. Select Version Control, and then select Git.
Clone the repository locally Paste the URL you copied into the Repository URL field. The Project directory name will automatically populate. Click Browse next to the Create project as subdirectory of field to choose where you want to save the folder on your laptop.
Initialise the project Click Create Project. RStudio will download the files from the main repository and open the new project.
Create a new branch In the RStudio Git pane (usually in the top right), click the New Branch icon (two purple squares and a white diamond). Give your branch a descriptive name (e.g., feature-data-cleaning), ensure “Sync branch with remote” is checked, and click Create. You are now working safely in your own isolated branch.





As others update the main branch, your feature branch does not synchronise automatically. Use this method to pull the latest changes into your workspace:

In the RStudio Git pane, use the branch dropdown (top right of the pane) to switch from your current feature branch to the main branch.
Click the blue Pull arrow (the down arrow) in the Git pane. This downloads the latest updates from GitHub directly to your laptop.
Switch back to your feature branch using the same dropdown menu.
Open the Terminal tab in RStudio (usually next to the Console) and type git merge main, then press Enter. This brings those new updates into your current branch.





If you and someone else edit the same lines of a file, Git triggers a Merge Conflict during a merge.

Identify the clashing files: In the RStudio Git pane, files with conflicts will display an orange U (Unmerged) icon.
Open the file: Click on the file in RStudio. Git will have added markers to show the clash:
<<<<<<< HEAD
Your local changes are here
=======
The updates from the main branch are here
>>>>>>> main
Edit the code: Decide which code to keep. Edit the text so the code looks exactly how the final version should work. You must delete all the <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers.
Save the file: Save your changes in RStudio.
Stage the fixed files: Go back to the RStudio Git pane and tick the checkbox next to the files you fixed. The orange U will turn into a blue M (Modified).
Commit to finish: Click the Commit button, leave the default merge message, and click Commit again to finalise the process.





Because Andre is working directly from the main branch rather than creating a separate feature branch, his workflow is simplified.


Andre follows steps 1 through 4 in Part 1 to clone the repository, but skips Step 5. He stays on the default main branch.



To get the latest updates from the main branch, Andre only needs to open his RStudio project, go to the Git pane, and click the blue Pull arrow.



After making edits and committing them, Andre can push his changes directly to the repository by clicking the green Push arrow in the Git pane. (If there are clashes with someone else’s recent push, he will resolve them using the steps in Part 3 before pushing).

title: ratpackR
text:
Do you have a fishery you need an MSE for – well RatpackR is your friend. RatpackR, developed by Andre Punt, is an extension of RatpackMSE a C++ package developed by scientists at CSIRO and earlier by Gavin Fay. The latest version includes the ability to evaluate management strategies in a multispecies context, including multispecies management strategies that attempt to explicitly account for multispecies interactions. RatpackR is being used in Australia, China and the USA.
This website hosts the documentation for the ratpackR software. It is still early days for the documentation, so thank you for your patience as we continue to build it.


One of the foundational programs underlying the original RatpackMSE software was Sinatra, a management strategy evaluation for Blue-eye Trevalla. CSIRO scientists such as Sally Wayte, Gavin Faye, Rich Little, and Andre Punt (among others) expanded that program to include multispecies technical interactions. When confronted with what to call this new multispecies version, the answer became clear: with more species than just Blue-eye, Sinatra will need the rest of his bandmates to form the full Rat Pack!
In short: a fish named “Blue-eye” Trevalla inspired the name Sinatra (i.e. Frank Sinatra) for an MSE software program and adapting it to a multispecies context (i.e. more than one musician) inspired folks to name the new software after the Rat Pack musicians (e.g., Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin, Sammy Davis Jr., Peter Lawford, and Joey Bishop).
